blocks.text: Let us put the whole chapter together on a small, concrete example, and watch what the machine does at each step.

This asks for one unbroken run of memory big enough for five numbers. Say it begins at address 2000 and each number takes 4 bytes — the block then runs from address 2000 up to 2019, and the array records 2000 as its base address.
The machine computes 2000 + 3 x 4 = 2012, reads the four bytes there, and gets 96. It did not examine slots 0, 1, or 2. One multiplication, one addition, one read.
Because the index is computed rather than typed, a loop can visit every element:

Each pass computes one address, reads one value, adds it to the running total. Five elements means five reads — and here the cost **does** grow with the size of the array, because we deliberately touch every element. That is O(N), and it is unavoidable when the answer depends on every value.

Notice the loop condition is `i < scores.length` and not `i <= scores.length`. With five elements the valid indices are 0 through 4, so the loop must stop *before* reaching 5. This single character is one of the most common bugs in all of programming.
Address 2000 + 1 x 4 = 2004, and four new bytes are written there. Nothing else in the array moves, because the slot was already exactly the right size. Instant.

items: An array is **one name for a run of adjacent, equally sized slots**.
The index is a **distance from the start**, which is why it begins at 0 and ends at length − 1.
`arr[i]` is **arithmetic, not searching** — base + i x size — which is why it is O(1).
**Reading by index and appending at the end are cheap.** Inserting or deleting in the middle is expensive, because the no-gaps rule forces elements to shift.

blocks.text: Every pattern in the rest of this course — two pointers, sliding windows, prefix sums — is built on these four facts. When a technique looks clever, it is usually just exploiting cheap indexing to avoid expensive shifting.
